evidence.claim: The Garnet Back Country Byway climbs 2,000 feet through the Garnet Range on a 12-mile journey to Garnet Ghost Town.
evidence.quote: The 12-mile long Garnet Back Country Byway climbs 2,000 feet through the scenic Garnet Range to Garnet Ghost Town.

evidence.claim: Evergreen forest accompanies the ascent, with views of the Blackfoot River Valley, Swan Range, Mission Mountains and Bob Marshall Wilderness.
evidence.quote: As the Byway climbs 2,000 feet into the evergreen forest of the Garnet Mountains, outstanding panoramas of the Blackfoot River Valley, the Swan Range, the Mission Mountains, and the Bob Marshall Wilderness come into view.

evidence.claim: Visit Montana identifies the ghost town as a major attraction of the byway; BLM emphasizes its preserved buildings.
evidence.quote: Garnet Ghost Town is a major point of interest along the Byway.

evidence.claim: BLM emphasizes its preserved buildings.
evidence.quote: Thanks to extensive preservation efforts, the 30 buildings in this historic town look much the same as they did in 1895.

evidence.claim: Driving the route usually takes 45 minutes.
evidence.quote: Driving time usually takes 45 minutes.

evidence.claim: Miners began prospecting in these mountains in the 1860s. A town grew beside a stamp mill built at First Chance Gulch in 1895, initially called Mitchell and renamed Garnet in 1897.
evidence.quote: Miners prospected in the Garnet Mountains beginning in the 1860s. When a stamp mill was built at First Chance Gulch in 1895, a small town grew up nearby. Originally named Mitchell, the town changed its name to Garnet in 1897.

evidence.claim: Its population rose and fell with the mines, and a fire destroyed much of the town in 1912.
evidence.quote: Population declined, rose, and declined again with the fortunes of local mines. A fire in 1912 destroyed much of the town.

evidence.claim: One thousand people lived here in the 1890s; the town was largely abandoned twenty years later when the gold ran out.
evidence.quote: One thousand people called Garnet home in the 1890s as they scoured the mountains for gold. Largely abandoned 20 years later when the gold ran out

evidence.claim: The remaining buildings have been preserved and are open to visitors.
evidence.quote: The remaining buildings have been preserved and are open to visitors.

evidence.claim: From Highway 200, take Garnet Range Road into the mountains toward Garnet.
evidence.quote: The Byway begins 30 miles east of Missoula where the Garnet Range Road leaves MT Highway 200.

evidence.claim: The town occupies First Chance Gulch amid mountains and forest.
evidence.quote: In First Chance Gulch in western Montana, the town is located 11 miles up the Garnet Range Road, in mountains and forest.

evidence.claim: The route ends at a junction with another BLM service road at Elk Creek.
evidence.quote: The route ends at its junction with another BLM service road at Elk Creek.

evidence.claim: The alternative approach from Bear Gulch is steep, narrow and rough.
evidence.quote: Follow signs up Bear Gulch for 11 miles to Garnet. This route is steep, narrow and rough.

evidence.claim: The byway begins where Garnet Range Road leaves Highway 200, thirty miles east of Missoula.
evidence.quote: The Byway begins 30 miles east of Missoula where the Garnet Range Road leaves MT Highway 200.

evidence.claim: The ascent gains 2,000 feet, carrying the byway into evergreen forest.
evidence.quote: As the Byway climbs 2,000 feet into the evergreen forest of the Garnet Mountains

evidence.claim: Views include the Blackfoot River Valley and the Swan and Mission ranges, as well as the Bob Marshall Wilderness.
evidence.quote: outstanding panoramas of the Blackfoot River Valley, the Swan Range, the Mission Mountains, and the Bob Marshall Wilderness come into view.

evidence.claim: The road also has a winter role: BLM marks and grooms the route for snowmobiles from January 1 through April 30.
evidence.quote: The route is marked and groomed for snowmobiles by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) from January 1 to April 30.

evidence.claim: Garnet belongs to a wider network of winter routes, with the 31.5-mile Garnet National Winter Recreation Trail System serving as the range’s winter recreation hub.
evidence.quote: The 31.5-mile Garnet National Winter Recreation Trail System is the hub for winter recreation in the Garnet Range.

evidence.claim: Winter access to Garnet from either direction is only by snowmobile, snowshoes or cross-country skis.
evidence.quote: Winter access from either direction is only by snowmobile, snow shoes, or cross-country skis.

evidence.claim: The steep, narrow and rough Bear Gulch approach is not recommended for trailers or RVs.
evidence.quote: This route is steep, narrow and rough. It is not recommended for trailers or RVs.

evidence.claim: Coloma is another ghost town in the Garnet Range, with a mining history that extended beyond a single boom.
evidence.quote: Coloma is a ghost town located in the area of the Garnet Range in Missoula County, Montana, United States.

evidence.claim: with a mining history that extended beyond a single boom.
evidence.quote: Additional prospecting activity occurred between 1932 and 1950.

evidence.claim: Records show substantial gold mining from 1896 onward. A mill was built in 1916, when further surveys examined the ore veins, apparently without success.
evidence.quote: Records of the period indicate high gold mining activity from 1896 onwards, with an estimated $200,000 to $250,000 in gold being extracted. In 1916, there was additional activity when a mill was built on the site and additional surveys on the ore veins were conducted, apparently without success.

evidence.claim: Further prospecting took place between 1932 and 1950.
evidence.quote: Additional prospecting activity occurred between 1932 and 1950.

evidence.claim: A stamp mill at First Chance Gulch gave Garnet its start in 1895.
evidence.quote: When a stamp mill was built at First Chance Gulch in 1895, a small town grew up nearby.

evidence.claim: The town had three hotels alongside grocery stores and a barber shop.
evidence.quote: as well as grocery stores, a barber shop, mercantile store, and three hotels.

evidence.claim: Hotel rates typically ran from one to three dollars; miners who could not afford them could pay a quarter to sleep in a windowless attic.
evidence.quote: Their rates typically ranged from $1–3, and the poor miners who could not afford that price could sleep in the attic without any windows for a quarter.

evidence.claim: The population reached as many as one thousand in 1898, but fell to three hundred by 1900.
evidence.quote: In 1898, as many as one thousand people lived in Garnet, but the boom was short lived. By 1900, three hundred people called the town home.

evidence.claim: A fire destroyed much of the town in 1912, adding another loss to the repeated rises and falls of its mining population.
evidence.quote: Population declined, rose, and declined again with the fortunes of local mines. A fire in 1912 destroyed much of the town.

evidence.claim: The surviving buildings are preserved under BLM management and open to visitors.
evidence.quote: The remaining buildings have been preserved and are open to visitors. The site is managed by the Bureau of Land Management.

flags: Cache lacks road-building history and a designation date; town development supplies historical context without claiming the road originated with the mill.

BLM says 30 preserved buildings look much as they did in 1895; the town article dates the founding mill to 1895 and describes a destructive 1912 fire. Dropped the current implication that all thirty buildings simply remained unchanged from 1895.
Current claim that the valley opens behind the road is not supported as a viewing direction; removed behind.
BLM describes the byway as reaching Garnet; Visit Montana places its endpoint at Elk Creek. Final paragraph retains the tourism office’s specific endpoint without equating it with the town.
Winter visitor-center details conflict across tourism and BLM pages; omitted. Winter access note reflects cached BLM guidance, checked offline on 2026-10-11.
Coloma is shorter because evidence is thin. Coordinates and strip order support its position before Garnet; cache does not establish current access or surviving structures.
